text.content:
Source: Camarilla Guide

The Camarilla is the oldest and largest sect of the Kindred, a coalition forged in 1493 out of the ashes of the Anarch Revolt. When the Convention of Thorns brought the rebellious childer of Europe back into the fold, the surviving elders known as the Founders built the sect around a single unbending principle: concealment. Motivated by the horrors of the Inquisition, the Camarilla made the Masquerade the centerpiece of Kindred existence, ending the age when vampires ruled mortals openly. In the six centuries since, the sect has endured as a bulwark against the Sabbat, the Lupines, mortal hunters, and its own internal rot, claiming jurisdiction over every vampire across the globe even as the Gangrel's recent, unexplained departure from the sect has shaken its foundations.

Camarilla society is bound together by the Six Traditions, the laws said to have been handed down by Caine himself. The First Tradition, the Masquerade, forbids revealing Kindred nature to those not of the Blood, on pain of death. The Second, Domain, grants a Kindred authority over his own territory. The Third, Progeny, forbids siring a childe without a prince's leave. The Fourth, Accounting, holds a sire responsible for the deeds of an unreleased childe. The Fifth, Hospitality, requires a visiting Kindred to present himself to the ruler of any city he enters. The Sixth, Destruction, reserves the right to end another Kindred's unlife to the elders, chiefly through the prince's power to call a blood hunt.

Authority in a Camarilla city flows from the prince, the supreme local ruler who governs domain, grants the right of creation, and holds the power of the blood hunt. The prince is advised by the primogen, a council of a city's clan elders whose influence varies from court to court, and relies on a seneschal as second-in-command to handle the routine business of rule. A sheriff enforces the Traditions and the prince's proclamations, while a scourge hunts down unpresented outlaws and Sabbat infiltrators, often with a free hand to destroy them. The keeper of Elysium maintains and secures the city's sanctified meeting grounds, and the harpies sit at the center of Kindred society, arbiters of gossip and reputation whose judgments can make or break a Kindred's standing. Above the cities stand the justicars, one for each clan, who carry out the will of the mysterious Inner Circle for a term of thirteen years and who may call a conclave, a sect-wide gathering, to address matters of grave importance; each justicar may in turn appoint archons to act as servitors bearing her authority.

Court life among the Camarilla is a study in formality and pageantry. Newcomers to a city must seek out Elysium, present themselves to the seneschal, and await an audience with the prince before they dare speak freely among the local Kindred, and those who linger unpresented risk the sheriff's or scourge's attention. Elysium itself, any site so designated for its cultural or artistic significance, is sacrosanct ground where violence and the use of Disciplines are forbidden, allowing rivals to mingle, scheme, and posture without bloodshed. It is in these halls that the Camarilla's true character is on display: a society of elders and their childer bound by ritual, precedent, and the careful, ever-watchful preservation of the Masquerade above all else.
